parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Picture the experiment - a beam of heavy, positively charged alpha particles fired at very thin gold foil. Think about what happened to the vast majority compared to the tiny few.
Hint 2: Link each observation to structure - what does passing straight through tell you about empty space, and what does bouncing straight back tell you about where mass and charge must be?
parts.proper_answer: Most alpha particles passed straight through with little or no deflection, showing most of the atom is empty space. A very small proportion were deflected through large angles greater than 90 degrees, showing mass and positive charge are concentrated in a very small nucleus.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Visualise What Most Particles Did**
Imagine firing thousands of alpha particles at gold atoms. Almost all of them go straight through as if nothing is there. That can only happen if atoms are mostly nothing - empty space with no mass or charge to block or repel the alphas.

Step 2: **Visualise What The Few Did**
A tiny fraction, about 1 in 8000, bounce right back towards the source. An alpha particle is heavy and fast, so to turn it around you need a head-on hit with something even heavier and very concentrated, and with strong positive charge to repel it. This tells you almost all the mass is packed into a tiny nucleus.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Think about how alpha and beta are particles with mass and charge, and contrast that with gamma - does it have mass or charge, and what family of waves does it belong to?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Remember What Gamma Is Not**
Alpha is a helium nucleus and beta is an electron, so both are matter particles. Gamma is completely different - it has no mass and no charge and is not a particle of matter at all.

Step 2: **Place Gamma In The Right Family**
Gamma is part of the electromagnetic spectrum, like light and X-rays but with even shorter wavelength and higher photon energy. So you can simply say it is electromagnetic radiation.

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Start by sorting by interaction - remember leptons are fundamental particles that do not feel the strong force, while hadrons do feel the strong force and are made of quarks.
Hint 2: Within hadrons, recall that baryons are made of three quarks. Think about which of neutrino, neutron and positron are fundamental and which is made of three quarks.
parts.proper_answer: neutrino: lepton only; positron: lepton only; neutron: baryon and hadron (not lepton).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot The Two Leptons**
Leptons are fundamental, not made of quarks. The neutrino is a classic lepton, and the positron is the antiparticle of the electron, so it is also a lepton. Neither feels the strong force, so neither is a hadron or baryon.

Step 2: **Spot The Baryon-Hadron**
The neutron is made of three quarks ($udd$), so it feels the strong force. Anything made of quarks is a hadron, and anything made of three quarks is specifically a baryon. So the neutron gets two ticks: hadron and baryon, and no tick for lepton.

parts.label: (d)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Focus on units - you have mass in kg but need it in u. Recall how one u is defined in kg from your data sheet and think about whether you need to multiply or divide to go from a very small kg number to a number near 1.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use The Conversion Between kg and u**
One unified atomic mass unit is defined as $$1\text{ u} = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$$ To change kg into u, divide the kg mass by this value:

Step 2: **Calculate To Three Significant Figures**
$$\text{mass in u} = \frac{2.19 \times 10^{-27}}{1.66 \times 10^{-27}} \approx 1.32$$ So the mass is $1.32\text{ u}$ to three significant figures.

parts.label: (d)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Remember this particle is a hadron, and with this mass it must be a baryon. Think about how many quarks make a baryon and how their charges must add up to give +2e.
Hint 2: List in your head the quark charges - which flavours carry +2/3 e and which carry -1/3 e? Work out what combination of three could total +2.
parts.proper_answer: Baryon of 3 quarks each of charge +2/3e, e.g. uuu. Any combination of up, charm, top quarks, e.g. uut, ccc, gives total charge $3 \times (+2/3e) = +2e$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why It Must Be Three +2/3 Quarks**
A hadron made of quarks with this mass is a baryon, which means 3 quarks. Total charge must be $+2e$. The only way with three quarks is: $$\frac{+2}{3}e + \frac{+2}{3}e + \frac{+2}{3}e = +2e$$ So each quark must have charge $+2/3e$.

Step 2: **Pick Allowed Flavours**
The quarks with charge $+2/3e$ are up ($u$), charm ($c$) and top ($t$). The down, strange and bottom quarks have $-1/3e$ and cannot be used. So any three from $u, c, t$ works, simplest is $$uuu$$ meaning three up quarks.
